title: Naval’s Recommended Reading
coreMove: Choose reading by live curiosity and mental-model yield instead of finishing lists for self-improvement status.
sourcePressure: The source opens by saying reading is not for self-improvement but for curiosity and interest. Its many recommendations point toward connoisseurship, theory, concepts, nonfiction, philosophy, science fiction, blogs, and sources that reshape how the reader sees reality.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version summarizes famous books or tells readers to read more. This chapter must turn the recommendation list into a reading method: follow appetite, seek explanatory power, abandon prestige reading, and build taste across fields.

counterintuition: the best book is the one you will read
tryThisNow: pick any book from your shelf

exampleSpecs.domain: marine insurance analyst abandoning a trendy business bestseller for a hard book on complex systems
exampleSpecs.audience: a professional who needs better explanations, not another finished title
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether she learns to price cascading port risk or merely completes the popular book everyone cites
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she closes the bestseller at chapter two, opens the marked complexity chapter, and writes one question about why small delays become system-wide losses
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A cargo-loss report lies beneath a half-read business hardcover.

exampleSpecs.domain: animation director using physics essays to solve a believable falling-cloth problem
exampleSpecs.audience: a creative reader who discovers theory through a live craft problem
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the scene stays fake because the team keeps guessing from reference footage
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she pauses the render, sketches the force path from the physics essay in the margin, and changes the cloth rig because the explanation finally predicts the motion
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A gray cloth simulation freezes mid-fall on a render monitor.

exampleSpecs.domain: rural judge reading Stoic letters between hearings to clarify anger rather than to collect quotes
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader under public pressure who needs an operating idea, not literary polish
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether contempt from one hearing bleeds into the next decision
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he copies one line into the case margin, shuts the book, and uses it to delay a sharp remark when the next attorney begins
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A paperback spine is cracked beside a stack of small-claims files.

exampleSpecs.domain: teen robotics captain skipping the assigned leadership book to devour a manual on gear ratios
exampleSpecs.audience: a young builder whose curiosity is more honest than the team's approved development plan
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether reading feeds the machine she is actually trying to build
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before the team meeting she hides the leadership book, after a failed climb she opens the gear manual to the torque table and fixes the lift ratio
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stripped aluminum gear lies beside a bookmarked torque table.

exampleSpecs.domain: restaurant fermenter reading microbiology because a batch of miso keeps collapsing
exampleSpecs.audience: a craft worker learning to follow the question rather than the prestige of the title
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether curiosity moves from recipe imitation to causal understanding
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he predicts the salt ratio is wrong, reads the microbial growth curve, tests the next crock, and changes the process because the concept explains the smell
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A ceramic crock is labeled with a salt percentage and a sour smell note.

exampleSpecs.domain: civil-rights exhibit designer using science fiction to make visitors feel future institutional choices
exampleSpecs.audience: a curator who normally reads only history but needs sharper imagination about systems
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the exhibit becomes dates on a wall or a model of how societies choose futures
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she moves a science-fiction paperback beside the exhibit flowchart, labels the imagined institution that made the story feel plausible, and redesigns one visitor choice around that model
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A worn science-fiction paperback sits open beside an exhibit flowchart.
mustAvoid: museum object from ch02 or ch03

skillTargets: distinguish curiosity-led reading from completion-driven reading
choose a book by the live problem or question it can illuminate
recognize when a difficult theory book is worth staying with
analyze how fiction, science, philosophy, and blogs can build different mental models
evaluate a reading practice by changed perception rather than number of books finished

tryThisNowSpec: Look at the last thing you genuinely wondered about today. Pick a source that might explain that one question, read until the question changes shape, and stop before turning it into a completion task.

sourceAnchors.name: David Deutsch
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names The Beginning of Infinity and says it is difficult but made Naval smarter
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Deutsch is the hard-book test: difficulty earns its place only when the explanations change how you think.

sourceAnchors.name: Yuval Noah Harari
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Sapiens as a dense history of humanity that changes how readers view history and other humans
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Harari’s Sapiens is useful here because one book can become a new lens on the whole human story.

sourceAnchors.name: Randall Munroe
sourceAnchors.detail: the source praises Thing Explainer for explaining complex systems with only the thousand most common English words
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Munroe proves that simplicity is not the enemy of depth; if the idea is clear, plain words can carry it.

sourceAnchors.name: Richard Hamming
sourceAnchors.detail: the source recommends Hamming’s You and Your Research as an old-timer essay on how to do great work
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Hamming belongs where reading stops being intake and starts becoming a question about the work you are avoiding.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following 'concrete anchor -> abstract rule -> elaboration'
